title.en: The case for and against interviews

hook.en: An interview can reveal a person's thoughts to millions of readers. It can also pry into a private life. Which is it?

body.en: Some see the interview as a supreme source of truth and, in practice, an art. Silvester quotes the view of the writer Denis Brian that, thanks to *interviews*, more people know more about their contemporaries than ever before. Interviews let readers hear a person's ideas in their own voice, and at their best they are thoughtful conversations.

points.en: A source of truth and, at its best, an art
Denis Brian: we know more about our contemporaries
Readers meet people through their own words
The interviewer holds great power and influence

say.en: Some call the interview a source of truth; others call it an intrusion.
At its best it is an art, but it can wound and diminish people.
It helps us know our contemporaries, but some feel it steals a part of them.
The interviewer is powerful, and that power can be misused.

body.en: Others regard the interview as an unwarranted intrusion into private life. Some feel it diminishes them. Silvester links this feeling to the belief in some cultures that taking a person's photograph steals that person's soul. In the same way, celebrities may feel that each interview takes something away from them.

points.en: A feeling of being diminished or exposed
Comparison: a photograph seen as stealing the soul
The interviewer's power can be misused

problem.en: Is the interview a source of truth or an intrusion? Present both sides.

steps.en: For: a supreme source of truth, an art, a way to know contemporaries.
Against: an intrusion; celebrities like Kipling and Naipaul felt hurt.
Explain the power of the interviewer in shaping a public image.
Conclude: its value depends on how fairly it is done.

answer.en: The interview can be both: a valuable source of truth and an art in good hands, but an intrusion and a wound when it ignores privacy. Its worth depends on the interviewer's fairness.
